questions.q: What is an eval set, as defined in this lesson?
options: A list of every possible user input a system could ever receive
A single example used once to demo a prompt in a meeting
A curated collection of representative input cases, each paired with a defined expected result, used to measure prompt behavior
The system prompt itself, renamed
questions.explain: An eval set is a curated set of cases with defined expected results — the thing everything else in this chapter (automated testing, A/B testing, regression testing) measures against.

questions.q: Why is an eval set built only from easy, common cases a problem?
options: It will pass almost any reasonable prompt, making it useless for catching regressions
It takes too long to run
Common cases are not allowed in eval sets
It requires too much storage space
questions.explain: A set of only easy cases won't distinguish a good prompt from a flawed one, since even a weak prompt would likely pass all of them.

questions.q: In the real eval case shown ({id, category, input, expected_behavior}), what does the expected_behavior field represent?
options: The literal text the user typed
A unique identifier for the case
The name of the model being tested
The defined standard the actual output is graded against
questions.explain: expected_behavior (or an exact expected output, for cases with one correct answer) is the standard used to judge whether the model's actual response passed.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should happen to an eval case created from a real reported failure once that failure is fixed?
options: It should be deleted immediately since the bug is fixed
It should remain permanently in the eval set as a regression tripwire
It should be renamed but kept hidden
It should only be used once and then discarded
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that a case exposing a past failure becomes a permanent fixture, so future prompt changes can't silently reintroduce the same failure.

questions.q: Where does the lesson say eval cases should primarily come from?
options: Cases invented at a desk based on what seems interesting
Randomly generated text with no connection to real usage
Real production inputs and real reported failures, not hypothetical examples
Only from the model vendor's official documentation
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that eval sets built from real logged usage and real failures better reflect actual behavior than cases a developer imagines might be interesting.
